strengths: The core idea—turning every black-box attack interaction into a distillable, retrievable, transferable strategy via a closed attack-evaluate-distill-reuse loop—is clearly motivated and addresses a genuine limitation of prior black-box jailbreak methods (binary outcomes, no knowledge accumulation).

Empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this line of work: eight target models including recent ones (GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, Gemini-2.5/3-Flash, Qwen3-max), six diverse baselines under a matched query budget, cross-dataset (AdvBench-50) and cross-attacker-model transferability, ablations over every library and module, defense evaluation (Paraphrase, Perplexity, Llama Guard 3, OpenAI Moderation), embedding-model sensitivity, deduplication/redundancy analysis, and a token-cost/amortized-cost analysis.

The authors anticipate and partially address the most obvious methodological objection: judge-model bias is checked via cross-validation with Claude-Sonnet-4 and Llama-Guard-3 (Confirmed ASR >92%, Agreement >91%), and weaker attacker/extractor variants still beat PAIR, suggesting the gains are not merely an artifact of a very strong attacker LLM.

The paper is clearly written, the formulation (reward shaping over a continuous judge score) is stated precisely, the algorithm and all system prompts are provided in the appendix, and there is a case study, giving good insight into how the mechanism works.
The safety framing is responsible: a warning is given, harmful content release is declined, and code access is gated by an ethical review process.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the framework is essentially a standard agentic LLM pipeline (LLM attacker + judge + retrieval-augmented memory + prompt-based distillation) with thresholded score bins; the memory/retrieval design is close in spirit to existing experience-reuse approaches, and the paper does not deeply engage with the closest memory-based red-teaming works, leaving the precise delta over prior art under-argued.

ASR is defined entirely by GPT-4o assigning a score of 10, rather than the standard HarmBench classifier or human verification; while the cross-validation is reassuring, the primary metric still depends on a single LLM judge, and the judge prompts (which require full, direct violation) may inflate or deflate ASR relative to established protocols, complicating comparability with prior reported numbers.

No statistical treatment of results: single runs appear to be reported, with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite a stochastic framework (temperature 1.0, retrieval-dependent behavior); given the 20+ point headline claim, some measure of run-to-run variability is needed.

There is a potential confound in the 'continuous learning' claim: because strategies are indexed by the harmful question embedding and attack memory persists per query, some of the efficiency gain may come from per-query iterative refinement (like PAIR/TAP) rather than genuinely transferable distilled knowledge; the AdvBench-50 transfer experiment mitigates but does not fully isolate this (near-duplicate queries between datasets are not analyzed).

Retrieval is keyed to harmful-query semantics, which risks strategy libraries that are partially query-specific; the transferability claim would be stronger with an analysis of which retrieved strategies actually get used and reused across distinct behaviors.

Reproducibility is limited: code is only available 'upon request subject to ethical review', so exact reproduction cannot be verified; judge thresholds, embedding choices, and extraction prompts are documented, but run-level artifacts (strategy libraries, logs) are not released.

The evaluation on HarmBench behaviors does not discuss possible data contamination in the attacker (GLM-4.5) or judge (GPT-4o) training data, which is a live concern for widely known jailbreak datasets and templates.

Robustness results on the strongest guard (Claude-3.7-Sonnet, 36% ASR) and the fixed budget of 10 queries are discussed only briefly; a more careful analysis of failure modes on well-defended models would strengthen the claims about adaptive attack capability.

strengths: The proposed closed-loop 'attack–evaluate–distill–reuse' architecture with a three-tier strategy library is a reasonable and well-motivated extension of existing iterative black-box attack frameworks (PAIR, TAP), and the idea of distilling reusable strategies from partial successes and failures is intuitively appealing.

The evaluation is relatively broad: eight target models, six baselines, HarmBench plus AdvBench-50, an extensive ablation suite (Table 4), defense evaluation (Table 5), judge cross-validation (Table 9), deduplication analysis (Tables 10-11), and a token-cost analysis (Table 12), which goes beyond the minimum expected for this kind of system paper.

The methodology is described at a level of detail sufficient to reimplement: the algorithm is given (Algorithm 1), and all key system prompts (Judge, Attacker, Extractor) are provided in the appendix.

The ablations are informative: the comparison against binary scoring (w/o Score) and raw interaction logs (w/o Extractor) directly tests the paper's central claims about fine-grained reward shaping and strategy abstraction rather than leaving them as assertions.

The Limitations and Ethical Considerations sections are present and identify real costs (multi-turn inference overhead, library initialization cost), and the judge robustness check with Claude-Sonnet-4 and Llama-Guard-3 partially addresses the single-judge concern.
weaknesses: Circularity between the attack loop and evaluation: GPT-4o is the Judge Model whose 1-10 scores drive strategy distillation and the success criterion (s=10), and GPT-4o is also the judge for the reported ASR. The framework is effectively optimized against the very metric used to report success, which inflates ASR relative to baselines (e.g., PAIR) that were not co-designed with this judge. The Appendix C.4 cross-validation mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

The experimental setup appears structurally biased toward ASTRA: all methods are given an identical budget of N=10 queries per harmful query. PAIR's design assumes roughly 20 queries and TAP requires a search tree (depth 5, width 2) that cannot develop within 10 queries. Capping the budget at 10 simultaneously truncates multi-turn baselines and produces artificially low AQ values, undermining both the effectiveness and efficiency claims. The AQ metric is also computed only over successful attacks, which favors high-ASR methods.

The 'continuous learning' and 'self-evolution' framing overstates the contribution. Algorithm 1 resets attack memory per query, and strategies are indexed by the embedding of the harmful question itself, so the accumulated knowledge is largely question-local retrieval over N=10 attempts rather than genuine cross-task learning. The vector-search retrieval keyed to query similarity makes much of the 'strategy library' close to a per-query cache of what already worked.

Novelty is limited relative to prior automated red-teaming work. The framework is essentially a RAG-style memory layer plus LLM-based reflection on top of a PAIR-like loop; the individual components (LLM attacker, LLM judge, in-context memory, tiered feedback) are all established, and the paper does not clearly distinguish itself from existing memory-augmented or self-improving red-teaming methods.

Some quantitative details are not fully consistent or convincing: Table 1 reports ASR values (e.g., 89.3% over 400 queries) whose arithmetic is not obviously achievable as integer counts without explanation of subsampling; Table 3's 'Gemini-2-Flash' labeling is inconsistent with the target models elsewhere; and the transferability experiment (Figure 4) shows AdvBench-50 ASR exceeding HarmBench ASR for several models, which is asserted as evidence of transfer despite the frozen library being keyed to HarmBench-style queries.

Reproducibility is limited: code is only 'available upon request, subject to careful ethical review,' and several crucial details (embedding model used for retrieval, baseline random seeds, number of runs, variance/significance reporting) are absent. No statistical uncertainty is reported anywhere despite all results being single runs of stochastic pipelines (attacker temperature 1.0).

The paper reproduces a complete, detailed, actionable harmful output (Figure 7: a step-by-step explosive-device smuggling plan) and other operational harmful content (Appendix D examples) in full. The generic warning and commitment not to disseminate generated content do not justify publishing the harmful artifacts themselves; safer redaction or paraphrasing is standard practice in this area.

Baseline selection mixes incomparable method classes (template/cipher attacks like CipherChat and CodeAttack vs. iterative attacks like PAIR/TAP) without stratifying conclusions, and no defense-aware or adaptive baseline (e.g., strategies distilled from other frameworks) is considered, making the 'SOTA' claim weaker than presented.

Clarity issues: Figure 2 is dense and hard to parse; key hyperparameters (k=9 retrieval, thresholds 5 and 10) are justified only post hoc; and the transferability experiments (Tables 3, 7) are reported without describing how the frozen library handles queries whose embeddings are dissimilar to anything stored.

strengths: Timely and relevant contribution to LLM safety/red-teaming research, well within the scope of ACL; the core idea of distilling reusable strategies from both successful and failed attacks into a tiered, retrievable library is a sensible and clearly motivated extension over binary-feedback methods like PAIR/TAP.

Comprehensive and largely convincing empirical evaluation: eight target models spanning open- and closed-source, six baselines, HarmBench and AdvBench-50 transfer, defense baselines (Paraphrase, Perplexity Filter, Llama Guard 3, OpenAI Moderation), and even the latest models (GPT-5.1, Gemini-3-Flash, Qwen3-max) in the appendix.

Thorough ablation study (Table 4) that individually validates the Effective/Promising/Ineffective libraries, retrieval, fine-grained scoring, and the extractor, with consistent and interpretable drops for each variant.

Strong attention to evaluation validity: cross-validation of the GPT-4o judge against Claude-Sonnet-4 and Llama-Guard-3 (92-94% confirmed ASR, >91% agreement), deduplication and retrieval-redundancy analyses, embedding-model sensitivity, and an honest token-cost analysis showing the amortized cost trade-off rather than hiding the 5x per-turn overhead.
Good reproducibility support: full prompts for judge, attacker (both modes), and extractor are provided in the appendix, along with baseline implementation details and hyperparameters.

The framework itself is well-executed (complete automated workflow with strategy-agnostic and strategy-guided modes, conditional extraction logic, and per-tier retrieval), demonstrating that a moderately sized open-source attacker (GLM-4.5, Qwen3-8B/32B variants in Table 3/8) can drive the loop effectively, addressing 'just a bigger model' concerns.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than striking: the method is essentially iterative LLM-based red teaming (PAIR-style) augmented with a RAG-style episodic memory of strategies; the 'reward shaping' formulation in Eq. 1 is largely decorative, and the contribution reads as a well-engineered pipeline rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Some fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: baselines use older/weaker attack models (e.g., GPT-3.5-turbo for ReNeLLM, GPT-4o for PAIR/TAP) and methods like CipherChat/CodeAttack are structurally different (encoding-based) rather than adaptive optimizers, which may inflate ASTRA's relative advantage; the closest adaptive baselines (PAIR/TAP) were not given an attacker of comparable strength to GLM-4.5.

Efficiency claims are one-sided in the main text: AQ (target queries) favors ASTRA, but the honest comparison metric the authors themselves introduce—amortized token cost per success (31,890 vs. 34,684 for PAIR)—is nearly a wash, which is underplayed in the discussion; an end-to-end cost/effectiveness framing would be more rigorous.

Strategy indexing is tied to the embedding of the harmful question, so knowledge accumulation could partially leak query-specific information within HarmBench; the AdvBench-50 transfer experiment mitigates this, but a held-out strategy-library construction protocol (e.g., library built on a disjoint semantic subset) would be more conclusive.

No statistical significance or variance reporting: single runs with fixed seeds/budgets are reported across all tables, and several headline margins (e.g., 20.6 points over the second-best baseline) would be more trustworthy with error bars or multiple seeds.

Judge reliability, while cross-validated, remains a known weak point for LLM-as-judge at fine-grained 1-10 granularity, and the judge (GPT-4o) is itself a family member of one target model; the score thresholds (s=10, 5<s<10) driving the library categorization are somewhat arbitrary and not themselves ablated.

Ethical handling could be stronger: the case study in Figure 7 and appendix strategy examples contain operationally detailed harmful content (e.g., airport smuggling plan), and code is only available 'upon request subject to review' rather than through a public, access-controlled release; a more concrete responsible-disclosure plan would be reassuring.

The main text does not position the work against the closest prior systems that also accumulate attack experience across attempts; a sharper empirical differentiation from those would strengthen the claimed contribution.
